explanation: No single theme. It fires on many unrelated tokens: code assignment operators (' =' after a variable), '::' namespace separators, digits inside citation or DOI IDs (e.g. B7-nanomaterials-02-0[[0]]113), URL path slashes, the comma after the weekday in email 'Sent: Monday,' headers, and occasional prose words such as ' to'. The common thread is a structured or code-like context, but which token fires is hard to predict.

Fires on mid-word or function tokens across many languages and contexts: Japanese/Chinese particles and characters (の, 、, 有), Russian word pieces, English subword continuations (Glob, ucle, it), and assorted numbers and prepositions. There is no clear lexical or semantic pattern.

A mixture. The strongest consistent part is ' even' after a negation ('didn't even', 'never even', 'not even'). Other parts are quantity and proportion words ('a fourth of', '1 percent', '2%'), the 'pone' journal prefix in citation keys (@pone.0...), and some URL and boilerplate tokens.

Fires inside synthetic algebra word problems and LaTeX math. The strongest hits are on equation-structure tokens: ' =', ' Suppose' starting a new clause, the space before a number term, and variable names in 'Solve ... for g'. It fires weakly on sentence punctuation and on license boilerplate in other text.

No coherent pattern. It fires on word-completion pieces (compl-acency, raref-ied, hit-and-m-iss), variable tokens in algebra problems (-0[[*g]], 4*[[o]]), legal 'Before' headers, closing quotes, and various prepositions in prose.

Fires on the second token of a word broken into pieces, especially the piece 'ag'/'Ag'/'Mag' (S-ag-ittarii, M-ag-ickWand, Mag-icka, Aug-mented, m-ag-rittr, Mag-dalen), and similarly on 'Tri', 'ac', 'Tab'. Mostly in proper nouns and technical names. A few compass words ('East', 'south') also fire.

Fires on single-letter variables or symbols inside LaTeX math, especially right after an opening brace or operator ('\mathbb{[[R]]}', '\mbox{[[H]]}', '}[[e]]^{-inx}', '+[[x]]^{n-2}'). It is moderate on other single capital letters and abbreviations and on some license boilerplate.

Mostly unrelated pieces: the fraction or half part of mixed numbers ('2 1[[/]]2', '6 1/[[2]]', 'one-and-a[[-half]]'), the middle subword of medical terms ('period[[ont]]al', 'enter[[ic]]', 'midg[[ut]]'), the second word of named titles ('Street Fighter', 'Wizard of Oz'), and ' source' in the Go license header.

Fires on word-piece tokens in the middle of rare proper names and identifiers, especially surnames split into subwords ('Over[[be]]a', 'Tol', 'Rif', 'P[[rie]]be', 'Sch[[wen]]k'), CamelCase code identifiers ('AD'atabase, 'Adj'acents), and digits inside citation or strain IDs. It is weak on ordinary words.

A mixture with no clear common thread. It fires on code keyword or value tokens ('line' in a chart config, 'import (' in Go, 'units' in boost include paths), the second word of fixed phrases ('Terms and Conditions', 'Franklin St', '24th Street', 'Boston Ave'), and subword pieces of technical terms.

Fires on the word 'engage' and its forms (engage, engaged, engagement, Engages, disengagement, unengaged) in every sense: combat, romantic, mechanical, and taking part. It fires weakly on look-alike subwords ('eng', 'og' in Cogload/Toggen). It is near zero on other tokens.

Two jobs. (1) Number and variable terms at the end of an expression in synthetic algebra problems ('+ 15[[1]]1 for l', '9[[*l]] for l', '11[[*h]]'). (2) Tokens in source-file license and copyright header boilerplate ('All rights reserved', 'file except in compliance', '$Revision$', include guards).

Mostly fires on boilerplate and code-syntax tokens. Examples are the first digit of the FSF street address ('[[5]]1 Franklin Street', '[[6]]75 Mass Ave') and other license wording ('provided that', 'write to the'), XML/HTML or Angular attribute openings ('="', '"&'), and abbreviation letters inside parentheses ((IC)D, (RS)V). Moderate on other punctuation.

Fires on the head word or subword that completes a technical compound term ('numerical aperture', 'cystic fib-rosis', 'amyloid precursor', 'highest common factor', 'hyperthy-roid', 'thy-rox-ine', 'worker's compensation'). It also fires on long digit strings and on 'COURT OF' in legal headers. Mostly the term-completion job, with unrelated extras.
